Good morning Raminder,
 
I have now had a chance to look at this. My thoughts are below:-
 
General Advice
 
My advice is as follows:-
 

Clearly in a perfect world obtaining an employee’s consent/ buy in to any sort of change is always preferable – however in my view this is
not necessary here and I entirely understand and appreciate why we would not want to have to do this in any event;The reason why consent is
not necessary is:-


Clause 4.2(c) of their contracts of employment requires each of them during their employment to “comply with all reasonable and lawful directions given to the Employee
 by the Company” – in my view working with Martyn Day on ongoing litigation which they have been working hand in glove with him on anyway for several years for a trial that starts next week is a reasonable and lawful direction;Clause 4.2(b) of their contracts of employment requires each of them during their employment to “diligently
 exercise such powers and perform such duties as may from time to time be assigned to the Employee by the Company;” – this is the same point.Although my view is that Clauses 4.2 (b) and (c) adequately cover the point, there is an additional helpful provision at Clause 4.1 of their contracts which states “The
Employee shall serve the
Company as a
Senior Associate
and will report to
Legal Director or their nominee.” As such Martyn Day could be designated as the “nominee” for the purposes of their contracts.


Please note that there are additional relevant clauses in their contracts which they should be complying with e.g. “to
use
their
best endeavours
to promote,
protect, develop
and extend
the business of the Company.” Their actions are, in my view, in clear breach of this.Sarah Bingham’s reference to Clause 4.2(a) in her email is correct albeit she has spun the meaning for her own
 purposes – the business of the Company remains exactly as it was before and taking some direction from Martyn Day for the common good does not change that;The concept of working on a case with other individuals outside of the firm giving directions to them on a piece
 of litigation is hardly a novel concept – for example, presumably these individuals do work at the behest of external counsel? No consent is required for those arrangements.
 
Pallas’s Questions
 
Turning specifically to Pallas’s email of 8.39pm last evening and the relevant questions for us:-
 
3. I agree entirely with Pallas’s paragraph 3. If the employees were being seconded they would need to give specific consent but this is not a secondment and falls within the confines
 of their contracts of employment as explained above;
5.2. Given JLG and Gallagher’s behaviour to date, notwithstanding that Nick Johnson confirmed in writing to Alicia that he agreed to the case leads remaining employed by PG until
 the end of the trial, their ongoing behaviour suggests that they may still be manouevring to escape early. It is therefore essential that all communications with them continue the tone of Anna’s email to them of Saturday 4 October – i.e. respectful/ open to
 hearing their concerns (however ridiculous they may be) and avoiding any opportunity for them to argue that PG have somehow breached their contracts of employment. That is not to say that we cannot respectfully push back on their points. Pallas’s suggestion
 of a meeting is eminently sensible albeit that PG should bear in mind that the case leads may try and get a rise out of PG in that meeting on purpose to argue that there has been a break down in relations. On this point, given that the trial starts next week,
 is there any world now where the case leads could resign and hope to be working at JLG next week for the trial? Something to bear in mind. Something else to consider, if not already done, would be to offer each employee access to PG’s Employee Assistance Programme
 if it has one – this is because the employees say that they are all stressed – and would therefore demonstrate that you are acknowledging their “stress”.
 
AA Agreement
 

I understand that the word “solely” has been removed from the document. This is helpful in that it deals with one of their points. It also reduces the scale of the delegation
 of authority to LD which in turn reduces the scope for them to argue that there has been a breach of contract – albeit as explained above I don’t think there has been any such breach;Although I am loathe to suggest any more changes to the Agency agreement given that this needs to be approved by Leigh Day ASAP, in a perfect world a further enhancement could
 be to designate Martyn Day as the “nominee” in terms of the new reporting line of the Case Leads – so that the language matches up to their contracts of employment. This is
not essential however for the purposes of this Agency agreement – it would be enough to tell the employees that Martyn is the person  - or one of the people - they need to report to;Otherwise I have no more comments on the Agency agreement.
 
I hope that this helps but if you or Pallas or anyone else have any queries please do not hesitate to ask.
 
Best wishes
 
Charlie
 
PS Just seen your latest email come in. I will review that now

Alicia, this is our recommendation beneath. In short:

 

a.     
We can’t totally ignore the case leads

b.     
Tell LD (and counsel) the AA can’t be finalised before the PTR

c.     
Speak to LD after the PTR to make necessary changes

d.     
Then speak to case leads to tell them about changes, and for the rest they need to get with the picture

 

The emails back and forth with this team is getting us nowhere. We think there needs to be a meeting with them, attended by Alicia and Anna.
 That obviously can’t be before the PTR, so would need to be on Tuesday at the earliest. But it might even have to be Wednesday. We would prepare you for this.Their overwhelming issue is the delegation of work by LD to individual solicitors at PG. This has always seemed problematic to us, but LD
 would not budge. We presumed that in practice, things would continue to work as they have done up to now, and Martyn Day seemed to confirm that – but the language remains different.


To be clear, we are not conceding the principle that the case leads have the right to consent to this agreement – but they can’t just be ignored.


We consider (but should get it cleared by Clydes) that there is nothing inherently wrong or out of the ordinary with an employer telling an
 employee to do, for a limited period and for specific work, what a responsible third party tells it to do – as long as the employer continues to oversee and supervise (including in the SRA sense) the employee. So if the employer considers the employee is nor
 being directed properly, it can tell the employee not longer to follow the directions of the third party.But that situation is not precisely what we have, because of the word “solely” in the Agency Agreement, where it relates to LD’s supervision
 of PG personnel doing the Common Work delegated to them. That makes it appear that only LD will know what the PG employees will do, so PG can no longer supervise them.So what is the way forward? We suggest the following:


Tell LD (and counsel) now that we will not be able to agree the AA before the PTR, and that we will need to speak to them after the PTR. During
 that discussion, give them a summary of the case leads’ concerns, remind them that they want and need to work with the case leads, and the only way we can see this getting anywhere is if we drop the word “solely”. We must also tell them that (subject
 to Clydes agreeing this is acceptable) PG will let the employees know it is authorising them to do the work at LD’s direction on a limited basis (Common Work only), that PG will retain oversight and supervision, and if PG considers that any direction is improper
 (eg, a breach of regulations), it will have the right to rescind our instructions to the employees to follow LD’s directions. We see this as the only way forward. Since Natasha has already been in contact with Martyn, it may be that she needs to deliver this
 message.At the same time, have Clydes look at the case leads’ letter and the agency agreement (with and without the word “solely”) and get their view
 on the employment law aspects (and how far we can push things). Clydes should also confirm that they see no employment issues with the way we are proposing to resolve this (which should not be an issue). Raminder can draft an employment response, but it should
not be sent until we have reviewed it and determined if it should be sent, consistent with our strategy.


When you meet the case leads on Tuesday (?), therefore, you will hopefully be able to say PG has amended the agreement, it is clear PG remains
 their supervisors, and you can be super-robust about everything else.


We would also suggest that after that meeting, you have a follow-up with them and Martyn Day, but we have to make sure Martyn is on side before
 suggesting that.


As for the PTR, there is
no way we can agree the agency agreement (and any side letter) before then, so we will need to tell the court we’re in the final stages of agreeing it.Ben Williams KC should be told that the agency agreement is being finalised –if necessary, he can say that is being done in consultation with
 the case leads. He can say that the case leads will be working their notice, which ends 15/19 Dec, but shouldn’t say anything more positive than that.
Thanks
Matt

Subject: Re: LD Agency
 



Dear Anna, 



Thank you for your email. 



We have some overarching points to raise before addressing the points in your email regarding the Side Letter Agency Agreement (“SL AA”). 



First and foremost, we have raised serious and significant issues regarding how traumatic we, and the entire team, are finding this process and that we have genuine concerns
 for the mental health and well-being of our staff. We further flagged that the proposal creates a two-tier structure amongst the wider team, which risks alienating individual members of the staff. Your email worryingly does not address any of those concerns,
 nor does it even mention them. 



We also note that various junior staff within the NOx department have been enlisted to send out correspondence, including on weekends, relating to non-common work and non-PDD
 Trial matters (see, for example, an email from Hannah Varghese at 15.32 on Saturday, 4 October 2025). Requiring the most junior staff to become actively involved in non-common work issues, while on the other hand attempting to assert that “everything we
 have done or are intending to do is with the best interests of our clients as well as our staff in mind first and foremost” is simply unreal. Correspondence of that nature and related to non-common work should be sent by an individual not working on critical
 workstreams.  



Each of the case leads are committed to finding a co-operative solution to the issues that are being raised. That is why we are proactively engaging in discussions and, in aid
 of assisting the firm, why we have continued to raise points so as to avoid the firm falling foul of issues that they may otherwise be presented with, e.g. noting potential additional disclosure obligations re. documents referred to in witness statements.
 You also have said that you “welcome any specific input we wish to contribute”. This is difficult to contemplate as being a genuine offer in circumstances where a) the SL AA was provided by Leigh Day (“LD”), not you nor the Board, despite Pogust
 Goodhead (“PG”) being our employer; and b) where we have previously sought to provide input (e.g. meeting with Alicia Alinia at 18:00 Monday 29 September 2025) and you have not engaged with it. Instead, you have sent us an email that dismisses our concerns
 and informs us that our description of the SL AA is incorrect, while at the same time stating that your intention is for this email to now bring these discussions to a conclusion. This is neither helpful nor is it in the spirit of co-operation.  



For the avoidance of any doubt, we do not consent to the SL AA in its current form. No representations can be made to the Court at the PTR on 6 October that this has been put
 in place and is agreed. To the extent that you and the Board believe you can bind individuals named in the SL AA (or annexes) by virtue of it being a ‘firm decision’ we disagree for reasons set out below. Every individual subject to the agreement either does
 not consent to it (the case leads) or, as far as we are aware, has never seen any version of it and so is unable to have provided consent.  We accept of course, that Counsel can inform the Court (on 6 October or otherwise) that it is being drafted and the
 intention is that it will be put in place in due course.  



If we, as the collective case leads, are to work collaboratively with the Board and you, and HR, to establish how we can move forward amicably, then it requires serious engagement
 from you and the Board, and not a dismissal of our concerns.  



We trust that this email will allow for a more collaborative approach going forward. 



On the points in your email: 


1.                  
Purpose and Effect of the Side Letter 


You explained that PG’s proposed role is intended to operate “exactly as envisaged”
within the existing Pan-NOx AA framework, and that the SL AA will simply implement a delegation of common work from LD to PG personnel. If that were indeed the case, a separate SL AA would not be necessary; indeed, this accords with our own understanding
 that the new arrangement is entirely novel.  



 



You say this agreement is to “ensure that [we] can continue to work as currently on the existing work plans.” Having reviewed the SL AA, it is clear that it goes
 further than the delegation provisions in the Pan-NOx AA, and that is precisely why it requires a standalone agreement. The SL AA imposes materially different terms in at least two key respects: 



 



a.
Formal separation of supervision and control 



The SL AA introduces an unusual structure whereby PG personnel will perform common work solely under the direction of LD, but remain employed and supervised by PG. Indeed, we
 understand that the Board intends for PG personnel to carry out generic/firm-specific work under PG’s direction. This formalises a split between line management and professional control that is not addressed, let alone authorised, in the Pan-NOx AA. That agreement
 permits delegation of work to another firm, not delegation of the supervision of one firm’s employees to another while the employer retains all employment obligations. 



 



b.
Governance over PG’s internal personnel decisions 



The SL AA (via Annex B) requires LD’s consultation and agreement before PG can add or remove PG personnel from common work. That means PG cannot unilaterally deploy or reassign
 its own staff in this litigation without LD’s approval. This imposes external governance over PG’s workforce, a control that is not contemplated in the Pan-NOx AA and which cuts across PG’s autonomy as an employer. 



 



The SL AA changes the status quo in material ways such that it cannot be said that what is being proposed is “exactly what we have all been working under” or that “this will
 not practically change much day to day.”  



 


2.                  
Tension with Employment Contracts 


Because the SL AA goes beyond what is authorised in the Pan-NOx AA, it creates direct tension with the terms of PG employment contracts. You advise that “there will be no
 change to your employment contract” and that “consent by employees is not necessary for PG to execute the agency agreement.” We respectfully disagree. 



Clause 2(b) of the SL AA states that “PG Personnel shall perform such Common Work … solely under the direction of, and reporting solely to, Leigh Day.” This directly conflicts
 with multiple provisions that we presume appear in each individual employee contract: 


 

a.
Duty of obedience and supervision 

Under Clause 4/Duties of the employment contract (which we presume is a standard term of contract for all PG employees), PG employees are contractually required to comply with
 PG’s directions and report to PG line managers. They are to “devote the whole of their time, attention and abilities to the business of the Company.” The SL AA seeks to override that by imposing a structure in which we report solely to LD in respect
 of a major portion of our work, without any formal secondment or variation of contract. 

 

b.
Regulatory oversight 

The split between day-to-day supervision (by LD) and formal employment responsibility (by PG) creates regulatory ambiguity under the SRA Code of Conduct. Who is the supervising
 solicitor? Are there two supervising solicitors, one from Leigh Day and another from PG? Which firm bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with professional standards?  

 

These are not academic questions - they carry regulatory and indemnity implications.  

 

c. Consent and legal clarity 

The arrangement introduces a dual-control model, but without staff consent, proper transparency, or any framework setting out lines of accountability. As PG remains the employer,
 yet LD directs our work in practice, the legal and ethical basis for this arrangement is unclear, particularly when conflicts, confidentiality obligations, or errors arise. 


 


3.                  
Professional Indemnity Insurance Risk 
The SL AA structure also raises serious questions around insurance cover. If PG personnel are performing common
 work solely under LD’s direction (as the SL AA confirms), then it is not clear whose professional indemnity (“PI”) insurance would respond in the event of a professional error. This is in circumstances where PG remains the/our employer and is responsible
 for holding PI cover for its staff. But LD is envisaged as exercising the day to-day control and making the litigation decisions. The SRA expects supervision and insurance liability to be aligned. That is not the case here. 


 



This is not hypothetical. A clear example of this risk occurred this week when LD made a costs offer to the Mercedes Defendants without PG’s knowledge or approval from PG's
 insurer - despite the fact that PG personnel had prepared the underlying work. If that offer proves problematic, it is unclear whether PG or LD (or both) would be liable and, more importantly,
whose insurer would be on risk. That ambiguity creates risk for both firms and undermines the clarity of the delegation framework set out in the Pan-NOx AA. 



 



This is precisely why the Pan-NOx AA structured delegation at the firm level: to avoid splitting supervision and risk in a way that confuses accountability. The SL AA
 unpicks that structure and introduces unnecessary exposure. 



 



We refer you to 17(a) of the PTR skeleton argument filed by Mercedes where the Defendants have drawn the Court’s attention to this issue. 



 


4.                  
Client Consent 


If PG wishes for us and other PG staff to be instructed by, and report solely to, a firm other than PG, then this requires our express consent, and (we believe) the informed
 consent of the clients whom we act on behalf of (which will not only be just the clients of PG, but  may extent to all clients within every GLO if the work is to be Pan-NOx). If PG personnel are to carry out work on those clients’ cases under the direction
 of a different firm, the clients must be told who is supervising that work and must provide informed instructions to that effect. We refer you to Rule 1.4 of the Code of Conduct, which requires solicitors to ensure clients are in a position to make informed
 decisions about their representation. You cannot unilaterally impose this on us, or on any of the PG staff, nor PG’s clients as your email  suggests you can. 
 
You cannot unilaterally impose a change of supervisory firm on your employees or on the clients, as your email equally suggests. The assumption that this arrangement can simply be implemented without individual or client-level engagement is not supported by
 the regulatory framework. This concern is not novel: post our comments in this regard, this is also expressly identified in the skeleton argument filed by Mercedes at paragraph 17(b), where they raise the potential for regulatory impropriety in precisely these
 circumstances. 



Turning to other points specifically raised in your email:  


·               
You note that we are obliged to work our notice periods. Thank you for pointing this out again, although we note it is not consistent with representations that PG has
 made to the Defendants and Court that the timing of our last days are subject to ongoing discussion. You go on to say that once our notice period has expired, we are free to commence working for JLG, should we so choose. Collectively, none of us have informed
 you of our plans post-PG.  

 

·               
You have advised that LD and counsel have approved this solution. Please provide us with this correspondence (including the advice the firm has taken from counsel
 – as originally requested). We note that as per Martyn Day’s email on 3 October at 13.56 that “Alicia has asked that we leave these issues for PG to sort out with the team. We await the outcome of those discussions and so no need for the meeting this afternoon.”
 In circumstances where LD are waiting for PG to “sort out these issues with the team” and that they will “await the outcome”, we fail to understand how LD have approved the solution. 

 

·               
You advise that you are “now interviewing so with time this work-stream will be handed over”. Please explain which work-stream? Does this relate to non-common
 work? 


We repeat that we are keen to try and work together to find a collaborative solution to these issues, not least because of the importance of the upcoming PDD Trial beginning
 in a little over a week’s time and for which we are all deeply invested in and, in truth, where all of this is causing a huge and detrimental distraction. However, it is plain to us that the SL AA is plainly more than a simple delegation mechanism. It alters
 the control and supervision structure, restricts PG’s governance over its own staff, creates clear tension with employment contracts and regulatory obligations, and places work done on behalf of the PG clients under the instruction of an external law firm
 (without any proposal for client consent to be obtained). If there is to be a material change, it needs to be handled transparently and within a proper legal framework. We raise these points constructively and in good faith, with the shared goal of ensuring
 compliance and continuing to act in our clients’ best interests. 



We trust these concerns now demonstrate that the issues raised in the draft SL AA document need to be engaged with, and we look forward to hearing from you on those issues and
 how they can be addressed, such that we can move forward, together.   The Case Leads

STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL




Dear Richard, Toby, Dinah,




First of all, very nice to meet you by e-mail -- I am happy to be taking over from Michael on the Ford claim and Quantum, and look forward to working with you!




Michael is preparing an update for you regarding the PDD Trial which will be with you tomorrow. I will also send you an update on Quantum shortly. 




I write however in relation to another matter to request your instructions. This request is very similar to that in relation to Mr Gormley, whom Michael wrote to you about on 26 September. 




It has become apparent during the Sample Claimant process that one of the individuals nominated by the Defendants, Lisa Bottomley, issued two claims: one in her personal name (which is being handled by Pogust Goodhead), and one in the name of her company, Baby
 J’s Ltd (which is being managed by Leigh Day). Following review of the documentation that the client provided us, it has become clear that the appropriate claimant in this matter is Baby J’s Ltd, as it is the company that is the legal owner of the vehicle
 that is the subject of the claim being brought in this litigation.




Consequently, we have advised Ms Bottomley that she should proceed with the claim through Baby J’s Ltd and that the claim in her personal name must be discontinued.




Before we proceed with filing the notice of discontinuance, we respectfully seek your instructions to:





Discontinue Ms Bottomley’s claim in her personal capacity in the Ford Group Litigation; and
Remove Ms Bottomley from the Ford Group Register.

As with the previous discontinuance of Kenneth Gormley’s claim, we want to clarify that this action will not have any negative impact on the litigation overall. While the Defendants will be entitled to recover certain costs due to this discontinuance, it is
 likely that on account of the Anti-Avoidance Endorsement (AAE) these costs will be paid by the ATE provider, although we suspect they will reserve their right to seek these costs either form Pogust Goodhead, or from Ms Bottomley herself. This will not result
 in any financial liability for you or the other Claimants. The costs associated with this discontinuance are expected to be minimal, particularly as Ms Bottomley's claim is part of the broader litigation and the common costs will be shared across the entire
 group.




As we proceed with this process, we do not anticipate any immediate costs being incurred, and we will continue to monitor the situation closely. If you have any questions or would like to discuss this further, I am available to do so.




We kindly request your instructions to proceed with the discontinuance of Ms Bottomley's claim, as outlined above.




Kind regards,

STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL




Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,

 

I hope you are all well. We have finished the first week of trial on Ford and I have set out an update below. Greg Lewis, a partner at PG who is in copy,
 will write to you separately about quantum related matters.  As you will be aware from my update on 7 October 2025, I am leaving Pogust Goodhead and
Greg will also have conduct of this matter going forward.




Executive Summary




Overall, the Claimant team is content with how things have gone. You may recall I previously flagged certain potential issues with our mechanical expert
 prior to the trial. I am pleased to report that these concerns did not manifest themselves significantly to the detriment of the case. Mr Carder performed reasonably well under cross examination, provided balanced and well reasoned answers to questions put
 to him by the Defendants, and engaged in good spirits with the Judge, who appeared to very much enjoy his candour. 




Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has worked
 at Ford for the past 25+ years. 




Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform to
 a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase their
 output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects certain
 Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge the LNT
 of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due to be heard
 next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues. 




On day two, the Claimant software expert, Dr Markus Heitz then took the stand. As with the September hearing, the Defendants sought to criticise Dr Heitz's
 report that it duplicated work in the Mechanical expert report, and that it was beyond his remit of instruction. Dr Heitz performed well under cross examination. Ultimately, however, much of the software analysis was agreed between the experts and Dr Heitz's
 cross-examination was quite short. 




Day three and four




Day three opened with the Defendants cross examination of the Claimants' mechanical expert, Mr Dan Carder. Despite our reservations about Mr Carder, he equipped himself well over the course of the cross examination. 




The Defendants' counsel team, consisting of Neil Moody KC and Sonia Nolten KC, took turns to cross examine Mr Carder, with Ms Nolten cross examining him on SCR and other available alternative technology, while Mr Moody covered "everything else". The Defendants'
 cross examination seemed relatively light touch and they did not go into depth on much of Mr Carder's report. 




Mr Carder dealt with their questions well and enjoyed good humour with the Judge, Lady Justice Cockerill.  He came across genuine and authentic (which has been our experience of him) and the Defendants failed to probe Mr Carder on a number of tricky areas arising
 out of his report. 




Mr Moody took Mr Carder through general points of principle and his analysis of the testing results. Mr Carder rightly pointed out that he was only there to present the data and make general points about what the Defendants could have done, at one point observing
 that it was not for him to "design a new and compliant Ford vehicle for them".  There were some comments made by Mr Carder that were not ideal, including his stating that "less EGR does not necessarily mean more NOx" but this was anticipated by us as being
 an opinion that he would share and so we were unsurprised. 




Ms Nolten then took Mr Carder through the SCR technology, an area that the Claimants' case is not as strong on as other points. She made a number of observations and suggestions that Mr Carder agreed with which may be less helpful as we move into closing submissions.
 He ultimately did not agree with her suggestion that the modulation that Ford deployed was suitable  - a key point in our argument that Ford did not calibrate their vehicles appropriately. Ms Nolten also cross-examined Mr Carder about alternative technologies.
 Mr Carder performed well. 




The morning of day four had Ms Nolten finish her questioning on SCR and then move onto alternative technology, an area that Mr Carder performed well in. While he did not make any positive assertions about what alternative
 technology "Ford should" have been using in their vehicles, he was firm that "Ford
could" have been using alternative (and we say better) technology in their vehicles.
 The Defendants' line of questioning on this at times seemed to suggest that Ford should not be held to the same standard as other manufacturers who were deploying better technology, and we think the Judge took note of
 this. Mr Carder asked the same question of Ms Nolten as to "do you think that Ford couldn't do it if VW could" who declined to answer the question. 




He made a number of good points back to the Defendants in cross examination and, most importantly, the Defendants failed to interrogate him on a number of salient areas of his report which now means they go unchallenged and are accepted in evidence, which is
 important for the case. 




Our junior barrister, Ms Joanna Buckley, lead the cross examination of Prof Migliorero, the Defendants' software expert. Similar to Dr Heitz, given much of the evidence was agreed, his cross examination was relatively short, however Ms Buckley managed to get
 a number of key admissions and agreements out of Prof Migliorero, which are salient for the overall case, and important for the cross examination of Ford's mechanical expert, Professor Frederico Millo, which commences on Monday. 




It transpires that Prof Migliorero is a former student of Prof Millo and they have worked together closely over the years. Ms Buckley, in cross examination, put to Prof Migliorero that certain paragraphs in his and Prof Millo's reports were identical. Prof Migliorero
 confirmed that the wording was from his report, and it was in fact, incorrect, which we imagine will make for a mildly embarrassing position for Prof Millo come Monday when his examination commences. 




Ms Buckley elicited from Prof Migliorero that software updates and the expansion of how the ECS operates were done within the constraints of the existing hardware but the main piece was that he confirmed the reports were prepared in concert.

We are 4 days through 6.5 days of evidence on Ford, and so far, it appears that the wind is blowing in our favour. The Judge will take her own view on the evidence and submissions, and we still have to hear evidence on PCD, Renault and Nissan, but it seems

Week 3 and 4: Mercedes




Following the previous updates, please see below update regarding the Mercedes portion of the trial which ran from 29 October until 6 November. 




There is significant correlation between Ford and Mercedes, as indeed there is across each of the 5 lead manufacturers, in that the technology that each manufacturer used is broadly similar i.e. they all used one of, or a combination of, the following types
 of technology; exhaust gas re-circulation ("EGR"), Lean NOx Traps ("LNT"), selective catalytic reduction ("SCR") and diesel particular filter ("DPF"). Each manufacturer used these technologies and strategies to varying degrees and
 in different ways with different calibrations and to differing levels of success. This in itself is helpful for our claim as their arguments and the reality of how they used the technology variously cut across each other as to the component limits or availability
 of technology at the time of use (some of the defences advanced by the Defendants).  It also helps us show that there was fundamental and systemic deliberate behaviour to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world driving compliance, despite the protestations
 of the Defendants. 




Week 3: Mercedes Mechanical Engineering Evidence (29-30 October) 

The third week focused on the Claimants' and Mercedes’ mechanical engineering evidence concerning the principal emissions control technologies installed in its cars to control the levels of NOx . These are EGR and SCR, which reduces NOx levels by converting
 it into water and nitrogen. The Claimants' mechanical engineering expert, Mr Juston Smithers was cross examined by counsel for Mercedes. We consider that he did well and withstood three days of cross-examination in a professional and knowledgeable way. 

Since Mercedes did not call factual witnesses, the examinations concerned expert evidence only. This, in our opinion and in our submissions to the Court, is quite illuminating.


Claimants’ Expert: 



Mr Juston Smithers (the Claimants' mechanical expert) demonstrated that EGR was programmed to operate at a higher rate during test conditions (and thus meet the emissions limits), with EGR downrating (performing to a significantly lower effectiveness level)
 outside of test conditions leading to higher NOx. 


Mr Smithers explained that Mercedes’ SCR system showed reduced effectiveness during extended idling or stop-start driving, causing elevated NOx in urban conditions, outside the levels permitted under the regulations. 


He argued that Mercedes’ safety justifications were speculative and unsupported. 





Mercedes’ cross-examination of Mr Smithers: 



Ms Helen Davies KC (the barrister for Mercedes) challenged Mr Smithers’ qualifications and data analysis. 


She claimed that any EGR downgrading was due to safety and ammonia slip concerns, which Mr Smithers disputed and which he advised were unsupported by contemporaneous documents. Such concerns, he said, would not justify Mercedes’ calibration choices such that
 the calibration choices were not immediately lead by these concerns but were instead likely lead by other considerations such as production cost.   


Mr Smithers was questioned about his analysis of NOx levels before and after Mercedes’ software updates, which showed large unexplained differences in emission levels. He concluded these variations were linked to changes in Mercedes’ calibration strategy, rather
 than random variation. 


 

Week 4: Mercedes Software and Mechanical Engineering Evidence (3-6 November)  

Week four saw further cross-examination of the Claimants' experts, Dr Heitz (software engineering who is the same expert in Mercedes and Ford, as he is for all of the cases for the Claimants) and Mr Smithers and of the Defendants’ expert witnesses, Dr John
 Martens (software engineering) and Raoul Spencer Day (mechanical engineering).

The Claimants' counsel team focused on the internal engineering and software design choices within Mercedes-Benz vehicles, arguing these revealed deliberate calibration to pass laboratory tests at the expense of real-world compliance. The Defendants’ experts

Claimants’ Experts: 



Dr Heitz and Mr Smithers confirmed that Mercedes’ SCR system used different dosing modes in tests and in real driving conditions, with higher AdBlue dosing — and therefore lower NOx — only under test conditions.   


The Claimants' experts’ position was that Mercedes’ firmware and calibration choices aligned with test-cycle boundaries (notably the NEDC 20–30°C temperature range) and that NOx emissions rose sharply just outside these parameters. This confirmed “cycle recognition”
 behaviour. 


Defendants’ Experts: 



Dr John Martens & Raoul Spencer Day (Ricardo plc) were challenged over their objectivity as experts in this litigation, given their extensive work for car manufacturers and commercial ties to several Defendants. They confirmed such relationships.

He accepted that US models used more effective emission hardware, with EU models prioritising fuel economy instead. This is positive for Ford given this is a tenet of our allegations against Ford.



Mercedes insisted these differences reflected regional regulations and safety trade-offs, not cheating, and claimed the Emissions Regulation applied mainly to type-approval tests rather than real-world conditions.

Statement of competence

 any learning needs in the past year. For further information please see 
SRA
 Competence Statement
which sets out core standards all solicitors should be able to undertake competently.

Internal
 Declaration.

 development. 
 
Please complete this by Close of Business on Friday 17th October.
 
Opting In

Please note: if you choose not to opt in to the renewal, you will be responsible for renewing your own practising certificate.

I am writing regarding the Pan-NOx Emissions Litigation, specifically regarding the viability of securing additional LOI coverage through further excess layer insurance
 policies.


Following the handing down of the judgment (10th September 2025) after the Second Costs Management Hearing (15-16 July 2025), the Defendants have revisited their
 position on applications for security for costs. We have therefore undertaken a further review of the potential adverse costs resulting from the Tranche 3 Quantum Trial and the Second General Budget. 


Previously, our assessment of ATE sufficiency was calculated on the following basis:



60% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;



60% of the Defendants’ claimed budgeted costs; and



100% of approved future costs to Spring 2026.

50% of the Defendants’ claimed incurred costs;

100% of approved future costs to 31 July 2026.

Notice Period

 Pan-NOx CRO.

 permission to be entered into that CRO. This takes up to 5 working days. There is also a process for applying to be removed from each CRO which can, in itself, take some days.
